title: The giant white cloud at a NASA rocket engine test isn’t smoke: it’s steam

cover.alt: Seen from high up, a tall grey steel test stand beside a river and forest, with a stream of white vapour drifting from its base.
cover.credit: NASA Stennis Space Center · Public domain

body: At NASA’s Stennis Space Center in Mississippi, RS-25 engines are bolted into the Fred Haise Test Stand (once called A-1) and fired straight down. Their exhaust, at over 6,000 °F (about 3,300 °C), hits a **flame deflector** that turns it sideways out of the stand. To stop the deflector being destroyed, a water plant floods it with cooling water, and the heat flashes that water into steam. The steam billows out as a cloud often mistaken for smoke, and it can even condense and fall again as light rain.

slides.alt: Seen from high up, a tall steel test stand stands beside a river. An orange glow appears at its base and a huge cloud of white vapour bursts out sideways, rolling across the grass until it fills half the picture.
slides.caption: Stennis Space Center, 21 March 2023: an RS-25 engine lights up inside the Fred Haise Test Stand, and a wall of white steam rolls out across the site.
slides.credit: NASA Stennis Space Center · Public domain · excerpt

slides.question: During a test, up to how many US gallons of cooling water a minute does the stand get?
slides.explanation: Up to about 170,000 gallons a minute, roughly 640,000 litres, delivered at 225 psi. Most of it goes to keeping the flame deflector intact.

slides.heading: Seconds of RS-25 firing
slides.note: Tests longer than about 350 s need a barge that tops up the propellant tanks while the engine runs

slides.label: Space Shuttle main engine tests on this one stand, 1975 to 2006
slides.text: Built between 1964 and 1967, it first tested Saturn V second stages for Apollo. Since 2015 it has tested RS-25s, the shuttle’s engine design, now used on NASA’s Space Launch System.

slides.question: Why is so much water poured into the stand during a firing?
slides.explanation: The exhaust tops 6,000 °F. Water sprayed through the deflector’s 21 stacked water boxes keeps it from being damaged as it turns the blast sideways.

source.label: NASA Stennis: A-1 Test Stand fact sheet
